register.name: Medical emergency
register.frequency_sentence: Nearly every household like yours will have someone need emergency care in the next ten years (about 1.4 times a year).

sub_causes.name: Far from emergency care
sub_causes.note: Ambulances take about twice as long to reach rural homes (a median of about 14 minutes against 7).

sub_causes.name: Falls
sub_causes.note: Falls are a leading reason older adults need emergency care; clear floors and light the way at night.

register.name: Cold wave
register.frequency_sentence: Nearly every household like yours will go through a spell of dangerous cold in the next ten years.

sub_causes.name: Rolling blackouts in extreme cold
sub_causes.note: Gas supply and power plants fail in deep cold and the grid cuts power in rotation or for days (Texas, February 2021). Already in the county's outage record.

register.name: Wildfire smoke
register.frequency_sentence: Nearly every household like yours will go through days of unhealthy wildfire smoke in the next ten years.

register.name: Heat wave
register.frequency_sentence: Nearly every household like yours will go through a heat wave in the next ten years.

sub_causes.name: A blackout during a heat wave
sub_causes.note: When the power fails in extreme heat, air conditioning fails for everyone at once. It is the most dangerous combination; where it matters most it is a named scenario.

register.name: Phone or internet outage
register.frequency_sentence: Of 100 households like yours, about 95 (63 to nearly all) will lose phone and internet service for hours in a network outage in the next ten years.

sub_causes.name: GPS or radio disruption
sub_causes.note: Space weather or jamming can degrade navigation and timing. Keep a paper map for the way home.

register.name: Strong wind
register.frequency_sentence: Of 100 households like yours, about 92 (61 to nearly all) will lose power or have damage in a windstorm in the next ten years.

sub_causes.name: Derecho
sub_causes.note: A fast line of storms with hurricane-force gusts over hundreds of miles; outages can last days. Counted in the windstorm rate.

register.name: Supply chain disruption
register.frequency_sentence: Of 100 households like yours, about 86 (63–98) will find store shelves empty of things they need in the next ten years.

sub_causes.name: Fuel shortage
sub_causes.note: Gas stations run dry for days (the Colonial Pipeline shutdown, May 2021, and before hurricanes). It matters most with a generator or a long drive.

sub_causes.name: Cut off: an island or a single road
sub_causes.note: A bridge, ferry or the only road closes and the community is cut off for days. Plan for longer if that is you.

register.name: Winter storm
register.frequency_sentence: Of 100 households like yours, about 84 (67–98) will be snowed in or lose power in a winter storm in the next ten years.

sub_causes.name: Blizzard or lake-effect snow
sub_causes.note: Whiteouts or very deep snow close roads for days. Counted in the winter-storm rate.

sub_causes.name: Roof damage under snow
sub_causes.note: Heavy snow or ice loads a roof until it sags or fails. Counted in the winter-storm rate; clear flat roofs early.

register.name: Local water or gas outage
register.frequency_sentence: Of 100 households like yours, about 78 (50–95) will have a water main break or boil-water notice in the next ten years.

sub_causes.name: Toxic algae in the water supply
sub_causes.note: Algae toxins reach the treatment plant and a do-not-drink order follows (Toledo, 2014). Counted in the water-notice rate.

sub_causes.name: Gas main over-pressure or leak
sub_causes.note: Gas mains over-pressure or leak and homes must be evacuated (Merrimack Valley, 2018). If you smell gas, leave first, then call.

sub_causes.name: Water system failure for weeks
sub_causes.note: A treatment plant or system fails for weeks (Jackson, Mississippi, 2022; Asheville, 2024). The water targets use the county's drinking-water violations to size it.

sub_causes.name: Sewer failure
sub_causes.note: Pumps stop or mains break and toilets cannot be flushed. The sanitation supplies follow the water target.

register.name: Job loss
register.frequency_sentence: Of 100 households like yours, about 77 (64–91) will have someone lose a job in the next ten years.

sub_causes.name: Livestock or poultry disease
sub_causes.note: An animal-disease outbreak (bird flu in dairy or poultry) can hit a farm's income.

sub_causes.name: Recession layoffs
sub_causes.note: Layoffs cluster in downturns; the high end of the job-loss range is a recession year.

register.name: Medicine shortage
register.frequency_sentence: Of 100 households like yours, about 39 (18–78) will have a daily medicine they cannot fill for days or weeks because of a shortage in the next ten years.

sub_causes.name: Hospital supply shock
sub_causes.note: A key hospital supply runs short (IV fluids in 2024, after Hurricane Helene closed a plant that makes a large share of the country's supply) and planned care is delayed.

register.name: Ice storm
register.frequency_sentence: Of 100 households like yours, about 37 (27–54) will lose power or be stuck at home in an ice storm in the next ten years.

register.name: Eviction
register.frequency_sentence: Of 100 households like yours, about 33 (16–59) will be taken to court and ordered to leave their rented home in the next ten years.

register.name: A household member is arrested or detained
register.frequency_sentence: For households with people the ages of yours, the FBI's counts come to about 4 arrests for every 100 households a year (2023–2025). This counts arrests, not guilt or convictions, and one person arrested twice counts twice.

register.name: Chemical spill or release
register.frequency_sentence: Of 100 households like yours, about 29 (10–57) will be told not to drink the tap water, or to stay inside, after a chemical spill in the next ten years.

sub_causes.name: Release from a chemical plant
sub_causes.note: A plant that uses large amounts of toxic or flammable chemicals has a release or explosion (West, Texas, 2013). Counted in the chemical-release rate.

sub_causes.name: Train derailment with chemicals
sub_causes.note: A train carrying chemicals derails and burns or leaks; homes within a mile or two are evacuated (East Palestine, 2023).

sub_causes.name: Tanker truck spill
sub_causes.note: A tanker crash closes roads and may bring an order to stay inside nearby.

sub_causes.name: Pipeline rupture
sub_causes.note: A gas or oil transmission pipeline ruptures and burns or spills; nearby homes are evacuated.

sub_causes.name: Refinery, tank farm or port fire
sub_causes.note: A large industrial fire brings orders to stay inside and smoke for days.

sub_causes.name: Chemical spill into the water supply
sub_causes.note: A spill upstream of a water intake brings a do-not-use order for days (Elk River, West Virginia, 2014). Counted in the chemical-release rate.

register.name: Long illness in the household
register.frequency_sentence: Of 100 households like yours, about 26 (14–59) will have someone sick at home for weeks in the next ten years.

register.name: Civil unrest
register.frequency_sentence: Of 100 households like yours, about 26 (10–45) will live under a curfew because of unrest in the next ten years.

sub_causes.name: Unrest around elections
sub_causes.note: Protests, clashes or curfews around elections or political events.

register.name: Stranded in a vehicle
register.frequency_sentence: Of 100 households like yours, about 26 (10–63) will be stranded away from home by a crash, breakdown or shutdown in the next ten years.

sub_causes.name: Black ice or dense fog
sub_causes.note: Chain-reaction crashes and closed highways. Counted in the stranding rate.

sub_causes.name: Transit shutdown or strike
sub_causes.note: Buses and trains stop and commuters without a car are stuck. Counted for commuters who travel by transit.

register.name: Government pay or benefits stop
register.frequency_sentence: Of 100 households like yours, about 20 (5–52) will have SNAP or WIC payments stop in a government shutdown in the next ten years.

register.name: Cyberattack on services
register.frequency_sentence: Of 100 households like yours, about 18 (7–39) will lose pharmacy, payment or other services to a computer outage or cyberattack in the next ten years.

sub_causes.name: Critical software failure
sub_causes.note: A faulty update or cloud outage takes down hospital, airline, bank or 911 systems for a day or more (July 2024). Counted in this rate.

sub_causes.name: Card or bank payment outage
sub_causes.note: Cards, bank apps or cash machines stop for hours to days. Keep some cash in small bills.

register.name: Burst pipe or water leak
register.frequency_sentence: Of 100 households like yours, about 17 (10–26) will have a burst pipe or leak flood part of the home in the next ten years.

sub_causes.name: Sewer backup
sub_causes.note: Sewage backs up through basement drains; standard home policies leave it out unless you add sewer-backup cover.

register.name: Pandemic
register.frequency_sentence: Of 100 households like yours, about 11 (3–23) will live through a pandemic that changes daily life in the next ten years.

sub_causes.name: Mosquito- or tick-borne outbreak
sub_causes.note: Local dengue or West Nile spread brings spraying and advisories.

sub_causes.name: Local disease outbreak
sub_causes.note: Measles, hepatitis A or Legionnaires' in the community keeps people out of school or work. Check your vaccinations.

sub_causes.name: Bird flu (H5N1)
sub_causes.note: A candidate pandemic strain that so far passes from animals to people, not between people.

register.name: Break-in
register.frequency_sentence: Of 100 households like yours, about 10 (5–18) will have a break-in in the next ten years.

sub_causes.name: Identity theft and disaster scams
sub_causes.note: Accounts opened in your name, or fake contractors and FEMA impostors after a disaster. A credit freeze is free.

register.name: Death or disability of an earner
register.frequency_sentence: Of 100 households like yours, about 9 (5–14) will lose an earner's income to death or disability in the next ten years.

sub_causes.name: Death in the family
sub_causes.note: A family member who does not earn dies: funeral costs and time off work.

register.name: Flooding from rivers or heavy rain
register.frequency_sentence: Of 100 households like yours, about 6 (2–15) will have flood water reach their home in the next ten years.

sub_causes.name: Flash flood
sub_causes.note: Water rises in minutes on roads and near creeks; most flood deaths are people driving into it. Counted in the flood rate; turn around, don't drown.

sub_causes.name: Basement or street flooding in heavy rain
sub_causes.note: Drains overflow and water or sewage comes up into basements outside the mapped flood zone. It is the outside-the-zone part of the flood rate, higher with a basement.

sub_causes.name: Levee failure or overtopping
sub_causes.note: Counted on the dam and levee card, not here: leveed land is mapped outside the high-risk flood zone.

sub_causes.name: Ice-jam flood
sub_causes.note: River ice jams in late winter and backs water into riverside homes. Counted in the flood rate.

register.name: Hurricane
register.frequency_sentence: Of 100 households like yours, about 5 (3–10) will lose power or have damage from a hurricane or tropical storm in the next ten years.

sub_causes.name: Inland flooding from a tropical storm
sub_causes.note: A weakening hurricane can drop a foot or more of rain far inland (Helene in western North Carolina, 2024), cutting water service for weeks.

register.name: Regional blackout
register.frequency_sentence: Of 100 households like yours, about 5 (1–14) will lose power in a regional blackout that is not caused by weather in the next ten years.

sub_causes.name: Attack on power substations
sub_causes.note: Gunfire or sabotage at substations can cut power to a county for days (Moore County, North Carolina, 2022). Utilities report about 78 cases of attack, vandalism or theft a year, most with no outage (2019–2023).

sub_causes.name: Cyberattack on the grid
sub_causes.note: Hackers switched off parts of Ukraine's grid in 2015; no US case has cut power. Utilities report about 7 cyber events a year (2019–2023).

register.name: House fire
register.frequency_sentence: Of 100 households like yours, about 3 will have a house fire in the next ten years.

sub_causes.name: Carbon monoxide poisoning
sub_causes.note: Carbon monoxide from a furnace, generator or car builds up indoors, most often after storms when generators run too close to the house. Shown beside fires, not added to them; a CO alarm is the defence.

sub_causes.name: Lithium battery fire
sub_causes.note: E-bike, scooter and power-bank batteries can catch fire while charging; charge them where you can see them.

register.name: Lightning
register.frequency_sentence: Of 100 households like yours, about 2 (fewer than 1 to 6) will have lightning damage their home or cut their power in the next ten years.

register.name: Tornado
register.frequency_sentence: Of 100 households like yours, about 1 (fewer than 1 to 4) will have a tornado damage or cut off their neighborhood in the next ten years.

register.name: Coastal flooding
register.frequency_sentence: About 6 (3–17) in 1,000 households like yours will have coastal flooding reach their home in the next ten years.

register.name: Earthquake
register.frequency_sentence: About 4 in 1,000 households like yours will feel an earthquake strong enough to knock things off shelves in the next ten years.

sub_causes.name: Liquefaction
sub_causes.note: Wet, sandy ground turns to slurry in strong shaking; pipes and foundations fail. Water outages last longer where it happens.

sub_causes.name: Fire after an earthquake
sub_causes.note: Broken gas lines and low water pressure let fires spread after a big earthquake. Know how to shut off the gas, and leave it to the gas company to turn it back on.

register.name: Attack or threat closes your area
register.frequency_sentence: Between 1 in 1,100 and 1 in 71 households like yours would have an attack or threat close their area or its transit for half a day or more in the next ten years.

location_factor.label: The Detroit-Warren-Dearborn, MI urban area is one of the 44 urban areas FEMA funds for terrorism preparedness, chosen by the risk the Department of Homeland Security assigns them. It gets about 1.2 in 100 of the money, which is how this estimate weighs your area.

register.name: Nuclear power plant accident
register.frequency_sentence: About 1 in 2,000 (1 in 10,000 to 1 in 500) households like yours will be told to stay inside or leave after a nuclear power plant accident in the next ten years.

register.name: Sinkhole or ground collapse
register.frequency_sentence: About 1 in 4,500 (1 in 18,000 to 1 in 910) households like yours will have a sinkhole or ground collapse damage their home in the next ten years.

location_factor.label: About 11 in 100 of Wayne County sits on karst, limestone and similar rock that water can dissolve into caves and sinkholes. Not every karst area has sinkholes, so this is an upper guide.

register.name: Hail
register.frequency_sentence: About 1 in 6,600 (1 in 18,000 to 1 in 2,900) households like yours will have hail damage their home or car in the next ten years.

register.name: Wildfire
register.frequency_sentence: About 1 in 9,700 (1 in 60,000 to 1 in 2,900) households like yours will have to leave home or lose power because of a wildfire in the next ten years.

register.name: War with attacks on US infrastructure
register.frequency_sentence: Between 1 in 250 and 1 in 13 households like yours would lose power, water or phone service for days to attacks in a war in the next ten years.

location_factor.label: Your county has military sites, a big city, a port or a refinery nearby: the kinds of places attacks on infrastructure aim at.

register.anchor_sentence: Less likely than the death or disability of an earner (about 9 in 100 for you in the next ten years).
register.if_it_reaches_you: Outages of power, water or phones for days, and shortages across the country.

register.name: Financial crisis with bank closures
register.frequency_sentence: Between 1 in 200 and 1 in 11 households like yours would have banks close for three days or more in a financial crisis in the next ten years.

sub_causes.name: Your own bank fails
sub_causes.note: Insured deposits (up to $250,000 per person at each bank) move to another bank, usually within days. The FDIC counts about 23 failures a year (2001–2025), most of them small banks.

register.anchor_sentence: Less likely than a pandemic that changes daily life (about 11 in 100 for you in the next ten years).
register.if_it_reaches_you: Cards and bank transfers stop for days.
register.what_it_changes: Keep some cash in small bills (already in your plan) and a second account at another bank (free).

register.name: Very large volcanic eruption
register.frequency_sentence: Between 1 in 130 and 1 in 26 households like yours would live through a year or two of higher food prices after a very large eruption somewhere in the world in the next ten years.

sub_causes.name: A Yellowstone super-eruption
sub_causes.note: Devastation nearby and ash across much of the country. The USGS puts it at about 1 in 730,000 a year.

register.anchor_sentence: Less likely than a regional blackout (about 5 in 100 for you in the next ten years).
register.if_it_reaches_you: A year or two of higher food prices and some shortages.

register.name: Severe pandemic
register.frequency_sentence: Between 1 in 200 and 1 in 21 households like yours would live through a pandemic far deadlier than COVID-19 in the next ten years.

sub_causes.name: A natural pandemic as deadly as 1918
sub_causes.note: The 1918 flu killed about 675,000 Americans. Records of pandemics over four centuries give the chance.

sub_causes.name: An engineered germ
sub_causes.note: A germ made or changed on purpose. There is no record to count; it is part of the expert range.

register.anchor_sentence: Less likely than a hurricane or tropical storm (about 5 in 100 for you in the next ten years).
register.if_it_reaches_you: Months of disruption, strained hospitals and lost income.
register.what_it_changes: Nothing new: the pandemic row already sizes your food and medicine.

register.name: Severe solar storm
register.frequency_sentence: Between 1 in 2,100 and 1 in 40 households like yours would lose power for days to a severe solar storm in the next ten years.

location_factor.label: Your county is at a middle geomagnetic latitude (about 51°). Solar storms drive the strongest currents into long power lines nearer the magnetic pole, so the chance of a long outage here is about 1.6 times the national average. The ground's conductivity also matters and is not counted.

register.anchor_sentence: Less likely than a house fire (about 3 in 100 for you in the next ten years).
register.if_it_reaches_you: Power out for days, and longer where large transformers fail.
register.what_it_changes: Nothing beyond your power plan: a solar storm harms long power lines, not phones or radios.

register.name: Nuclear attack or EMP
register.frequency_sentence: Between 1 in 10,000 and 1 in 42 households like yours would be in a blast zone or under dangerous fallout in the next ten years.

sub_causes.name: Limited strike on US territory
sub_causes.note: One or a few weapons on US soil, for example a strike on Guam, Hawaii, Alaska or a West Coast base. It adds to your chance only where your county is a plausible target.

sub_causes.name: A crude nuclear device in a city
sub_causes.note: Heavy damage within about a mile, and everyone within 50 miles told to get inside. It adds to your chance by your metro area's share of FEMA's terrorism-preparedness money.

sub_causes.name: Electromagnetic pulse (EMP) from a high-altitude burst
sub_causes.note: Only as part of a nuclear attack: a burst high above the country could damage electronics and black out a region. EPRI's 2019 study found little damage to large transformers and did not support a nationwide blackout lasting months. The claim that most Americans would die rests on testimony that assumed such a blackout for a year, not on a published model.

sub_causes.name: Disruption across the country
sub_causes.note: Shortages, power cuts and lost income even far from any target. Shown for everyone and never added to your local chance.

sub_causes.name: A nuclear weapon used elsewhere in the world
sub_causes.note: At home: market shocks, shortages and worry, with no fallout of concern. Never added to your local chance.

location_factor.label: You live in the Detroit metro area: a metro area of more than a million people. Places like this could be targets in a large nuclear war, but they are less likely targets than the biggest cities and military sites.

register.anchor_sentence: Less likely than a house fire (about 3 in 100 for you in the next ten years).
register.if_it_reaches_you: Serious disruption: sheltering inside for a day or more against fallout, then shortages and outages.
register.what_it_changes: One free step: pick your shelter spot at home and at work (a basement, or the middle of the building away from windows).

register.name: Power out for months (any cause)
register.frequency_sentence: Between 1 in 18,000 and 1 in 39 households like yours would be without power for two months or more in the next ten years.

sub_causes.name: A severe solar storm
sub_causes.note: Long outages where large transformers fail; most places would be back within days.

sub_causes.name: EMP from a nuclear attack
sub_causes.note: Only as part of a nuclear attack; EPRI's 2019 study did not support a nationwide blackout lasting months.

sub_causes.name: Attacks on the grid in a war
sub_causes.note: Cyberattacks, sabotage or missiles on power plants and lines.

sub_causes.name: Your county's own outage record
sub_causes.note: Storms and failures like the ones in your county's outage records, with the long tail the records cannot show yet.

register.anchor_sentence: Less likely than a regional blackout (about 5 in 100 for you in the next ten years).
register.if_it_reaches_you: No power for months: water, heat, medicine and money all affected. Puerto Rico waited 328 days after Hurricane Maria.
register.what_it_changes: Nothing to stockpile for months. What helps instead: a way to treat water from a nearby source, a way to cook without power, a plan for toilets and waste, and some cash.

register.name: Chemical, biological or radiological attack
register.frequency_sentence: Between 1 in 81,000 and 1 in 410 households like yours would be told to stay inside, or to collect medicine at a public site, after a chemical, biological or radiological attack in the next ten years.

sub_causes.name: Chemical
sub_causes.note: A toxic chemical released on purpose: shelter inside for hours, or leave the immediate area if told to.

sub_causes.name: Biological
sub_causes.note: A germ spread on purpose (the anthrax letters of 2001): stay home, and collect preventive medicine at a public site if told to.

sub_causes.name: Radiological ("dirty bomb")
sub_causes.note: Shelter inside for hours; the area may stay closed for weeks.

location_factor.label: The Detroit-Warren-Dearborn, MI urban area is one of the 44 urban areas FEMA funds for terrorism preparedness, chosen by the risk the Department of Homeland Security assigns them. It gets about 1.2 in 100 of the money, which is how this estimate weighs your area.

register.anchor_sentence: Less likely than an attack or threat closing your area (about 4 in 1,000 for you in the next ten years).
register.if_it_reaches_you: An order to stay inside for hours, closed buildings, or medicine handed out at public sites.
register.what_it_changes: Nothing beyond your basics: your three-day supplies cover sheltering inside.

register.name: Mass shooting or bombing
register.frequency_sentence: Between 1 in 330,000 and 1 in 33,000 households like yours would have someone hurt in a mass shooting or bombing in the next ten years.

location_factor.label: The data are too sparse to say where this is more likely, so the chance is the same everywhere.

register.anchor_sentence: Less likely than a wildfire (about 1 in 9,700 for you in the next ten years).
register.what_it_changes: Nothing to buy. Two free steps: know "run, hide, fight", and learn to stop bleeding.

requirements.plain: 3 battery lights: a headlamp or lantern for each person aged 4 and over. Use lights, not candles. (Ready.gov; some amounts are estimates)
1 pack of AA or AAA batteries for the lights and the radio: one pack lasts a household about 7 days. Check which sizes your lights use. (Ready.gov; some amounts are estimates)

1 pair of appliance thermometers, one in the fridge and one in the freezer: after a power cut, keep refrigerated food only if it stayed at 40 °F or below, and throw out perishable food that was above 40 °F for 2 hours or more. (Ready.gov)

1 battery power station (about 1,070 Wh each) as an optional upgrade for lights, phones and a radio. Your essential load (phones) is about 30 Wh a day, 150 Wh for 5 days; one station gives about 910 Wh after losses, enough for about 30.3 days of that load. A full-size fridge alone would drain one in about 0.9 days. (retail prices, ENERGY STAR; some amounts are estimates)

Optional: a portable generator can run the fridge and lights through a 5-day outage. It must run outdoors, at least 20 feet from windows, doors and vents, never in a garage, and it needs fuel (see the fuel line). Ask your landlord first. (CDC, Ready.gov, Ready Reckoner research; some amounts are estimates)

Optional: keeping a fridge running takes about 995 Wh a day (a chest freezer about 597) × 5 days = 4,980 Wh. A closed fridge keeps food cold about 4 hours and a full freezer about 48; shelf-stable food avoids the need. (ENERGY STAR, Ready.gov)

For a boil-water notice of up to 10 days: make about 2.3 gallons of drinking water safe each day, about 22.5 gallons in all. To make it safe, boil it for 1 minute (3 minutes above 5,000 feet), or add 8 drops of 6 % unscented bleach per gallon (6 drops of 8.25 %) and wait 30 minutes; double the bleach for cloudy or very cold water. A gas stove can boil water while the gas flows; never use a camp stove or grill indoors. (Ready.gov, CDC, EPA)

1 bottle of plain unscented bleach (5 to 9 % sodium hypochlorite, not the splashless kind), for making water safe and for cleaning, however long your target is. At about 0.5 mL a gallon, each ounce treats about 60 gallons of clear water (30 if it is cloudy or very cold), so one bottle treats thousands of gallons. Bleach weakens in storage: buy a fresh bottle every 6 months, when you replace the water you store yourself. (CDC, EPA; some amounts are estimates)

If you boil on a camp stove outdoors, about 3.1 lb of propane brings 85 L to a boil (about 25 to 30 L a pound). Never use a camp stove indoors, and keep no more than 2 one-pound cylinders inside. (EIA, local fire code, CDC; some amounts are estimates)
3 people × 1 gallon a day × 5 days = 15 gallons. Replace water you store yourself every 6 months. (Ready.gov, CDC)

Free first step: fill clean drink bottles you already have with tap water, about 6 gallons, the most a household can usually gather this way. Not milk jugs: they leak. Label them and replace the water every 6 months. (Ready Reckoner research, CDC, Ready.gov, Church of Jesus Christ; some amounts are estimates)
A two-bucket toilet for when toilets can't flush: 2 sturdy buckets with a seat, one for pee and one for poo. (RDPO, Oregon OEM)

Toilet bags: about 0.45 heavy garbage bags a person a day (0.3 to 0.6), counting both bags of a double-bagged load: 3 people × 5 days = 7 bags. Fill halfway, tie, double-bag, and store away from food, water, children and pets. Don't put them in curbside trash or bury them unless officials say so. (RDPO, Oregon OEM; some amounts are estimates)

Cover material for the poo bucket (sawdust, shredded paper, dry leaves or pet bedding): about 1 cup a person a day (0.5 to 1.5) × 3 people × 5 days = 15 cups, about 0.9 gallons. (RDPO; some amounts are estimates)

1 adult at about 2,262 kcal a day, 1 person 65 or over at about 2,009 kcal a day and 1 child aged 4 to 12 at about 1,667 kcal a day: about 5,937 kcal a day × 21 days = 124,700 kcal. These are moderately active needs; the form does not ask sex, so men's and women's needs are averaged. Count calories, not servings. No agency sets a one-month amount: this step sits between the two-week advice (Red Cross, Oregon, Washington) and the Church's three-month pantry. (Dietary Guidelines, CDC, Red Cross, Oregon OEM)

As everyday groceries: about $558 for 63 person-days (USDA Thrifty Food Plan, $8.44 a person a day, plus 5 % for a household of 3). Buy what you already eat, keep it in the pantry and use the oldest first. (USDA)

As bulk staples such as wheat, rice and beans: about $158 ($2.15 to $2.85 a person a day). Cheapest, but it needs cooking and is short on some vitamins, so it suits months rather than days. (Church of Jesus Christ, BYU)

As freeze-dried or dehydrated meals: about $1,496 ($9 to $39 per 2,000 kcal, so $561 to $2,431). They need about 0.6 gallons of extra water a person a day to prepare. (Dietary Guidelines, retail prices; some amounts are estimates)

A retail "30-day" food kit supplies about 1,290 to 1,730 kcal a day. For the average person here (about 1,979 kcal a day) one lasts about 20 to 26 days, not 30. Compare kits by total kcal. (Dietary Guidelines, retail prices)

A way to cook without power, because your plan runs 21 days without a store, longer than food that needs no cooking comfortably covers: your gas range can boil water and cook while the gas still flows. If its igniter needs power, light a burner with a long match (check the manual first). Never use the oven or burners to heat the home. (Oregon OEM, CDC, Ready.gov; some amounts are estimates)

Fuel for a propane camp stove: about 0.2 lb of fuel a person a day × 3 people × 21 days = 12.6 lb, or 13 one-pound propane cylinders. Use the stove outdoors only (carbon monoxide), and store the cylinders outside the living space, with no more than 2 inside the home or an attached garage. (CDC, Ready Reckoner research, EIA, retail prices; some amounts are estimates)

Optional, if you have an outdoor gas grill: a spare filled 20-pound cylinder is the cheapest way to boil water and cook in a long outage. Use the grill outdoors only, away from the house, and keep the cylinder outside, never indoors or in the garage. (local fire code, CDC)
Toilet paper: about 1 roll a person every 5 days × 3 people × 21 days = 13 rolls. Better still, measure a week's use and double it for two weeks. (Oregon OEM; some amounts are estimates)
Soap for 3 person-months: 3 people × 1 month. Each is 250 g of bathing soap and 200 g of laundry soap, about 1,350 g in all. (Sphere)

Period products for 2 cycles each, about 20 products a cycle (15 to 30). The form doesn't ask sex, so the plan counts half of the 1 person aged 13 to 64 who are not pregnant or nursing: 1 cycle's worth, about 20 products. Keep soap, clean underwear and pain relievers with them, and put used products in a separate bag. (CDC, Sphere, Oregon OEM; some amounts are estimates)

2 battery fans: 1 for the home plus 1 for the 1 person most at risk from heat (65 and over, babies, pregnancy). Fans help only while it is below 90 °F indoors; above that, go to a cooling centre. (CDC; some amounts are estimates)
3 cooling towels, one for each person: wet them and wear them on the neck in a heat wave. (an estimate)
A heat plan: find your nearest cooling centre (dial 2-1-1), pick the coolest room, cover sunny windows, and agree who checks on whom. Never leave people or pets in a closed car. (CDC, Ready.gov)
1 room thermometer in the room where the most vulnerable person sleeps: fans help only while it is below 90 °F indoors, so when it reads higher, go somewhere cooler. (CDC)
3 warm blankets, one for each person: most homes already have them. (Ready.gov, Sphere)
3 sets of warm layers (coat, hat, gloves, dry socks), one for each person. (Ready.gov, CDC)

3 sleeping bags or extra heavy blankets, one for each person, rated for the coldest nights where you live: your cold target of 5 days is longer than the 3 days that blankets and warm layers cover. (Ready.gov, Sphere; some amounts are estimates)

A cold plan: pick one room to keep warm, close off the others, put towels under doors and cover windows at night, and find your nearest warming centre in case the home gets too cold. Never heat with a gas oven, grill, camp stove or generator indoors (carbon monoxide). Gas, oil and propane furnaces usually need electricity for their fans and controls, so plan for cold without power. People 65 and over should check the indoor temperature often. A body temperature below 95 °F needs medical help at once. (CDC, Ready.gov; some amounts are estimates)

1 person takes prescription medicine every day: keep 21 days of it on hand. Keep a written list of each medicine, what it is for and the dose. After a disaster declaration some states let pharmacies give an emergency refill of up to 30 days, and many allow only a few days; ask your pharmacist what yours allows. (Florida DEM, CDC, Red Cross, Healthcare Ready)

No antibiotics are included in this plan. If you have a specific, foreseeable need, such as remote travel, talk to your own clinician about a standby prescription with written instructions. Never use fish or pet antibiotics, never share prescriptions, and don't use expired ones. (CDC, FDA)
1 battery or hand-crank radio that gets NOAA Weather Radio, with a tone alert, for warnings when phones and power are down. (Ready.gov, NOAA)
Power banks: 2 phones × about 15 Wh a day (10 to 20) × 5 days without power = 150 Wh. Text instead of calling to save battery. (Ready.gov; some amounts are estimates)

2 two-way radios for the 2 people aged 13 and over, to reach each other when phones are down. FRS radios need no licence; GMRS radios reach farther but need a $35 FCC licence that covers the family for 10 years. (FCC; some amounts are estimates)
3 written contact cards, one for each person aged 4 and over: an out-of-area contact, meeting places and key numbers. Phones die; paper does not. (Ready.gov)
1 paper map of your area, marked with meeting places and ways out. Save offline maps on your phone too. (Ready.gov)

Cash in small bills, kept with your documents, because ATMs and cards may not work in an outage: about $120: half of 3 days of your usual spending ($2,400 a month), the part that goes on food, fuel and medicine. No agency gives a dollar amount. (Ready.gov, FEMA; some amounts are estimates)

3 go-bags, one for each person: a sturdy bag you already own will do. Pack copies of documents on paper and on a flash drive, a phone charger, cash, a flashlight, a whistle, an old pair of prescription glasses, a change of clothes and sturdy shoes, and add water, food and medicines from your home supplies rather than buying them twice. You may get only minutes of warning (a local tsunami or a fast fire), so keep the bags packed by the door, and one at work if you work in a danger zone. Practise grabbing them and leaving. Plan where you would stay for about 2 days. (Washington EMD, Ready.gov, CDC; some amounts are estimates)

Water for the go-bags comes out of the water you store at home, not on top of it: the Red Cross three-day supply for leaving home, about 3 gallons a day for the 3 people × 2 days = 6 gallons. Keep it with the bags or take it as you leave. If you leave on foot, carry what you can (about 2.5 L each) and a filter; the rest goes in the car. (Red Cross, Washington EMD, Ready.gov, CDC; some amounts are estimates)

Food for the go-bags comes out of your home food supply, not on top of it: about 5,937 kcal a day × 2 days = 11,900 kcal of food that needs no cooking or refrigeration. (Red Cross, Washington EMD, Dietary Guidelines)
No car: decide now who would drive you, or which bus or train leads out of the area, and leave early, because it takes longer without a car. (Ready.gov)
1 person may need help to leave quickly: arrange a ride and a helper now, and show them where the medicines and equipment are. (Ready.gov)

Person 1 travels 6.8 miles (11 km) by bus or train to work or school; walking home at about 3 mph takes about 2.3 hours. Keep a get-home bag at work or in your daily bag: comfortable walking shoes, a light, a paper map, cash in small bills, a rain or warm layer, and water and snacks from home. Be ready to stay at work for 24 hours if you can't leave. (FHWA, Ready.gov; some amounts are estimates)
Water for person 1's walk home: 2.3 hours × about 0.5 L an hour = 1.1 L, in a bottle filled from home rather than bought extra. (FHWA; some amounts are estimates)

Snacks for person 1's walk home: about 200 kcal for 2.3 hours on foot (about 1,250 kcal every 12 hours), from your food at home rather than bought extra. (FHWA, Dietary Guidelines; some amounts are estimates)

1 family first-aid kit for 3 people: the Red Cross list for a family of 4 (bandages, gauze, tape, antiseptic wipes, gloves, a breathing barrier, a cold pack, tweezers, an emergency blanket and a thermometer). Add your own medicines and emergency numbers, and replace what you use. (Red Cross)

2 packages of each of 4 kinds of non-prescription medicine (a pain reliever, an anti-diarrhea medicine, an antacid and an allergy medicine): one package of each lasts about 14 days for 4 people. That is 8 packages for 21 days. Follow the label, and ask a pharmacist about children's versions. (Ready.gov, CDC, Red Cross; some amounts are estimates)
1 oral thermometer (non-mercury, non-glass; it is on the Red Cross kit list). (Red Cross)

Oral rehydration salts for vomiting, diarrhea or heat illness: 3 packets a person for every 2 weeks, at least 2 weeks' worth. For 3 people and 21 days that is 14 packets. Mix each packet into 1 litre of safe water. (CDC; some amounts are estimates)
1 bleeding-control kit: a tourniquet and a pressure bandage for serious bleeding, and a Stop the Bleed class so you know how to use them. Serious bleeding can kill before help arrives. (DHS)

A wound-care and splint add-on for the first-aid kit: an irrigation syringe to wash a wound with clean water, wound-closure strips, an elastic wrap, a padded splint, trauma shears, blister dressings and gauze for packing a deep wound. Washing a wound out with plenty of clean water is the key step. Your plan runs past 14 days without a store, when a small wound has to be cared for at home. (Wilderness Medical Society, Red Cross; some amounts are estimates)

A fire escape plan: two ways out of every room, a meeting spot outside, and a practice run with everyone. Upstairs bedrooms need a second way out, such as a window onto a porch roof or an escape ladder (see the ladder line). A bedroom below ground needs its own second way out too, usually a window big enough to climb through. (Ready.gov)

No smoke alarms yet: one on every level and in every bedroom, about 3 levels and 2 bedrooms for a home like yours = 5 alarms. Ask your landlord first; if that fails, ask your fire department or the Red Cross, which install free smoke alarms in many places, and buy them yourself only if nobody can. Test them every month. (USFA, Ready.gov, Red Cross; some amounts are estimates)

No carbon monoxide alarm yet: put one on every level where people sleep (2 for a home like yours), with battery backup. Replace them every 5 years or as the maker says. (CDC, Ready.gov; some amounts are estimates)

No fire extinguisher yet: 2 multipurpose (A-B-C) extinguishers, one on each of the 2 floors a home like yours has, the ground-floor one near the kitchen. If your kitchen is on another floor, keep one there too. Learn how to use one before you need it. Small home fires are common: CPSC estimated about 6.6 a year for every 100 households, most of them cooking fires, and fire departments attend only about 3 in 100 of them. (USFA, CPSC; some amounts are estimates)

A house like yours usually has bedrooms upstairs (2 levels): 1 two-storey escape ladder for an upstairs bedroom window, in case fire or smoke blocks the stairs. Skip it if every bedroom is on the ground floor or already has a second way out, such as a porch roof. Keep it by the window and practise with it. (Ready.gov; some amounts are estimates)
Swap phone numbers with 2 neighbours and agree who checks on whom after a storm or an outage, when phones and roads may be down. (an estimate)

N95 respirators, for about 5 days of smoke, dust or ash: 1 a day for each of the 2 people aged 13 and over = 10 respirators. A well-fitting N95 protects far more than a cloth or surgical mask; replace it when breathing through it gets harder. Respirators are not made to fit young children (EPA): for them, the clean room is the protection. (CDC, EPA; some amounts are estimates)

1 portable air cleaner with a HEPA filter for your clean room: for a room of about 200 square feet, a clean air delivery rate (CADR) of at least 130 for smoke (EPA's sizing, more for high ceilings). Keep a spare filter, and avoid air cleaners that make ozone. (EPA; some amounts are estimates)

Cheaper than an air cleaner: a 20-inch box fan with a 20 by 20 inch MERV 13 filter taped to its intake side, which EPA calls a cost-effective way to cut smoke indoors. Use a newer fan with safety features, and do not leave it running while no one is home. (EPA)

A clean-room plan for smoky or dusty days: pick one room with few windows and doors where everyone can sleep, keep it closed, set the heating or cooling to recirculate (or turn off fans that pull in outside air), run the air cleaner there, and do not fry food, burn candles or vacuum on those days. Children stay in the clean room: respirators do not fit them. (EPA, CDC)

Savings goal: about 7 months of expenses ($16,800 at $2,400 a month), built up over time and kept apart from the supplies budget. You have about 0 months saved now. Planners often suggest 3 to 6 months; the CFPB says it depends on your situation. (FINRA, St. Louis Fed, CFPB)

Someone in your household earns money the others rely on: check whether your job offers disability insurance, and whether life insurance would carry the others through the years they would need. About 1 in 4 workers who start at 20 become disabled before retirement age. NAIC's buyer's guide helps you work out how much cover is enough. (SSA, NAIC)

Copy the 4 parts of FEMA's Emergency Financial First Aid Kit: IDs, financial and legal papers (including insurance), medical information, and household contacts. Keep copies in a waterproof, fire-resistant place or with someone you trust, with photos of your home and belongings, and update them once a year. (FEMA)
You have no renters insurance yet: get a quote and decide. Check what it pays if you have to live somewhere else for a while. (FEMA, Ready.gov)

Home and renters policies usually don't cover floods. Decide on flood insurance before you need it: Most homes in your county are outside the mapped high-risk flood zone, and that is where many uninsured floods happen: about 3 in 10 flood insurance claims come from outside high-risk flood areas. A quote costs nothing, and a new policy usually starts 30 days after you buy it. It pays up to $250,000 for the building and $100,000 for belongings, and renters can buy cover for belongings only. (FEMA, FloodSmart, Ready.gov)

# Your preparedness packet

**For:** 1 adult, 1 older adult and 1 child  
**Where:** Wayne County, Michigan (ZIP code 48227)  
**Home:** a rented house, with a basement, city water, gas heat and window air conditioning  
**Plan date:** October 1, 2026  
**Ready for:** very serious disruptions (the 1-in-100 setting), in today's climate. Water is planned at the basic level, about 1 gallon a person a day.[1]

> Ready Reckoner is an independent, open-source planning aid. It is not official emergency guidance, and not medical, legal or financial advice. Follow instructions from your local officials first.

## Summary

**Where you are now:** getting started. **What is enough for your risks:** one month of supplies. At your budget, the bare minimum (three days of water, light, warmth and medicine) is in place by month 8 (June 2027); the rest takes longer. Start with the free steps under Your plan.

### The three things that matter most

1. Of 100 households like yours, about 90 (85–100) will lose grid power for a day or more in the next 10 years. Be ready to manage about 5 days at home with no power or tap water.
2. Of 100 households like yours, about 70 (50–95) will be unable to shop for food and supplies for 3 days or more in the next 10 years. Keep about 3 weeks of food you normally eat, and 3 weeks of daily medicine on hand.
3. Of 100 households like yours, about 25 (10–40) will have an income gap of more than 3 months in the next 10 years. Losing a paycheck is the longest disruption most households face. Aim for about 7 months of expenses in savings over time, apart from this supplies budget.

**What the plan assumes you already have:** a charged mobile phone, go-bag for each person, manual can opener, a cooking pot with a lid, three days of the food you normally eat, a warm blanket for each person, warm layers for each person and towels to wet and cool down. If any is missing, untick "Assume everyday basics" on the Have screen and the plan will add it.

## Your family plan

This is the plan you wrote; fill in anything still blank together. Keep a copy in each go-bag and one on the fridge: phones die.[2]

| Plan | Ours |
| --- | --- |
| Meeting place near home | The front steps of the church on our corner |
| Meeting place outside the neighborhood | The branch library on Grand River Avenue |
| Out-of-area contact | Cousin Tanya in Columbus, 555‑0140 |
| Who picks up the children | Grandma, or Mr. Ellis if she cannot; the school only releases children to adults on its card |
| Work and school plans | Dee stays at work until the buses run, then comes home |
| Shelter spot at home | The inner hallway on the main floor, away from windows (not the basement in a flood) |
| Shelter spot at work or school | The loading-dock stairwell |
| Where we would go | Tanya's house in Columbus |
| First way out | Bus to downtown, then the Greyhound to Columbus |
| Second way out | A ride with Mr. Ellis on I-75 south |
| Neighbors who check on us | Mrs. Owens next door checks on Grandma; we check on her |
| Gas shut-off | At the meter by the side door; the wrench is on the shelf above it |
| Water shut-off | Basement, front wall, by the meter |
| Electrical panel | Breaker box at the bottom of the basement stairs |
| Lawyer | Legal aid office, 555‑0143 |

**Our trusted circle:** people who agreed to help, and what they hold for us.

| Name | Phone | Holds for us |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Tanya | 555‑0140 | a spare key, copies of documents |
| Mrs. Owens | 555‑0141 | a spare key |
| Mr. Ellis | 555‑0142 | medical power of attorney, backup codes |

**Numbers we know by heart:** 555‑0140; 555‑0141

### Leaving home

Of 100 households like yours, about 15 (9–25) will have to leave home quickly at least once in the next 10 years. Warning can be as short as a few minutes (a home fire) or as long as 12 hours. For floods from rivers and heavy rain, plan for as little as a few minutes of warning; for chemical spills and releases, a few minutes. Plan to be away for about 2 days. Most evacuations last a few days, but after a home fire you could be away for 2 months or more. With no car, plan to leave early when told to evacuate: arrange a ride or know the transit route.[3, 4, 5, 6, 7, 8, 9, 10, 11]

### Staying in touch

**Four ways to reach each other.** Emergency planners call this a PACE plan: a primary way, an alternate, a contingency and an emergency way. Each one takes over when the one before it fails.[12] For a household it can be:

1. Primary: call.
2. Alternate: text. A text may get through when a call does not, and it saves battery.[13]
3. Contingency: everyone texts one out-of-state contact, who passes the news along.[13]
4. Emergency: go to the place you agreed to meet if you get separated.[13]

**School and child care.** Every place your child spends time should have an emergency plan. Keep your contact details, the list of adults allowed to pick up your child, custody papers and medical needs up to date there. After an emergency, follow official directions about where to reunite.[14]

Cut out a card for each person's wallet or phone case.

## Your risks

What could reach a household like yours in Wayne County, Michigan over the next 10 years: the likeliest events, and the rarer ones that can kill, most likely first.

### What to know and do

#### 1. Medical emergency

Nearly every household like yours will have someone need emergency care in the next ten years (about 1.4 times a year).[15]

**Includes:** far from emergency care; falls.

**What helps.** Take a first-aid and bleeding-control class. You may be able to save a life by acting right after an injury, before help arrives.[16] If a teen or adult collapses and their heart stops, call 911 and push hard and fast in the center of the chest. This hands-only CPR needs no training. Note where the nearest heart defibrillator (AED) is; it talks you through each step.[17] Keep a stocked first-aid kit. Check it regularly and replace anything used or out of date.[18] Keep a list of each person's medicines, doses and allergies with your emergency supplies.[19] Know how to reach 911. Call if you can, and text where that service works.[20]

**What to avoid.** Do not start antibiotics on your own or take someone else's. The wrong medicine can delay the right treatment and cause serious side effects.[21] Do not use expired medicines.[22]

**How bad:** Serious (based on data).

#### 2. Cold wave

Nearly every household like yours will go through a spell of dangerous cold in the next ten years.[23]

**Includes:** rolling blackouts in extreme cold.

**What helps.** Keep extra blankets, sleeping bags and warm coats, and pick one room to keep warm.[24] If you cannot keep your home warm, go to a warming center. Dial 2-1-1 to find one.[25] Learn how to keep pipes from freezing, and test smoke and carbon monoxide alarms before winter.[26] Keep a car kit with jumper cables, sand, a flashlight, warm clothes, blankets, water and snacks, and keep the gas tank full.[26] Check on older neighbours often.[24] Know the signs of hypothermia, such as shivering, confusion and slurred speech. A body temperature below 95°F is an emergency. Warm the center of the body first.[26]

**What to avoid.** Never heat your home with a gas stove or oven. Use generators and grills only outdoors, away from windows.[26] Choose electric space heaters with automatic shut-off, and keep them 3 feet from anything that can burn.[24, 27] Do not overdo it when you shovel snow.[26]

**How bad:** Serious (based on data).

#### 3. Wildfire smoke

Nearly every household like yours will go through days of unhealthy wildfire smoke in the next ten years.[10, 28, 29]

**What helps.** If anyone has heart or lung disease, ask their health care provider now what to do on smoky days. If someone has asthma, make sure they have an asthma action plan.[30] Keep at least five days of food and medicine at home, so you can stay in.[31] When smoke is forecast, check the air quality on AirNow or your local news, and set up your clean room.[30] Staying indoors is the best protection. Keep two-strap respirators for anyone who has to go out.[32]

**What to avoid.** Avoid hard exercise while it is smoky.[30] Do not stay in a home that is too hot or still smoky inside: go to a friend's home out of the smoke, or a public cleaner-air shelter.[31]

**How bad:** Serious (mostly data).

#### 4. Heat wave

Nearly every household like yours will go through a heat wave in the next ten years.[23]

**Includes:** a blackout during a heat wave.

**What helps.** Know where you can go to cool off. Dial 2-1-1 to find air conditioning near you.[33] Cover windows with drapes or shades, and weather-strip doors and windows.[34] Take cool showers, wear loose, light-colored clothing, and drink plenty of fluids. Check on family members, older adults and neighbours.[34] Heat can cause power outages, so plan for refrigerated medicines and powered medical devices.[33]

**What to avoid.** Do not rely on a fan when it is over 90°F indoors. It can make you hotter.[33] Never leave people or pets in a closed car on a warm day.[34] Heat stroke is an emergency. Signs include a body temperature of 103°F or more, hot, red skin that may be dry or damp, a fast, strong pulse, confusion or passing out. Call 911, move the person somewhere cooler, cool them with cool cloths or a cool bath, and give them nothing to drink.[35]

**How bad:** Serious (based on data).

#### 5. Burst pipe or water leak

Of 100 households like yours, about 17 (10–26) will have a burst pipe or leak flood part of the home in the next ten years.[10, 36, 37]

**Includes:** sewer backup.

**What helps.** Find your main water shut-off valve now, and show everyone how to turn it off. A burst pipe can flood a room quickly.[38, 39] Once a year, check the hoses to the water heater, washing machine, dishwasher and fridge, and replace any that crack or leak. A leak alarm can warn you early.[38] In freezing weather, let a faucet drip at night, open the cabinet doors under sinks on outside walls, and keep the heat at 55°F or higher.[39] Home and renters policies usually cover burst pipes. Many do not cover a sewer backup unless you add that cover, and floods need their own policy.[38]

**What to avoid.** Never thaw a frozen pipe with an open flame; use a hair dryer. Watch for electric shock around standing water.[39] Do not leave home while the washing machine or dishwasher is running.[38]

**How bad:** Severe (mostly data).

#### 6. Flooding from rivers or heavy rain

Of 100 households like yours, about 6 (2–15) will have flood water reach their home in the next ten years.[9, 10]

**Includes:** flash flood; basement or street flooding in heavy rain; ice-jam flood.

**What helps.** Look up your address on FEMA's flood maps, and sign up for your community's warnings.[40] Homeowner's insurance does not cover flooding, and a flood policy typically takes up to 30 days to start.[40] Renters can buy flood coverage for their belongings.[41] Know how you would get to higher ground or a higher floor.[40]

**What to avoid.** Six inches of moving water can knock you down, and one foot can sweep your car away.[40] Never drive around barriers on a flooded road. The road may have collapsed under the water.[8] Stay off bridges over fast-moving water.[40] Leave if you are told to.[42]

**How bad:** Very severe (rough data).

#### 7. House fire

Of 100 households like yours, about 3 will have a house fire in the next ten years.[11]

**Includes:** carbon monoxide poisoning; lithium battery fire.

**What helps.** Put smoke alarms inside and outside every bedroom and on every level, and test them each month.[43] Practice your escape plan twice a year, including finding your way out in the dark.[44] Sleep with bedroom doors closed. Teach children not to hide from firefighters.[44] If there is smoke, crawl low under it to your exit.[44] If you cannot get out, close the door, cover vents and cracks with cloth or tape, call 911, and signal from the window with a light-colored cloth or a flashlight.[44] Insurance and copies of your documents help you recover afterward.[45]

**What to avoid.** Before you open a door, feel the door and the knob. If either is hot, or smoke is coming around it, keep it closed and use your second way out.[44] If a person or pet is still inside, get out and tell firefighters right away.[44] If your clothes catch fire, stop, drop and roll.[44]

**How bad:** Severe (based on data).

#### 8. Tornado

Of 100 households like yours, about 1 (fewer than 1 to 4) will have a tornado damage or cut off their neighborhood in the next ten years.[6, 10]

**What helps.** Pick your shelter spot now. A safe room or storm shelter is best.[46] The next best is a small, windowless room or basement on the lowest floor of a sturdy building.[46, 47] Sign up for your community's warnings, and learn what your sirens sound like.[46] Know the signs of a tornado: a rotating funnel cloud, a cloud of debris, or a roar like a freight train. In your shelter, protect your head and neck with your arms, and pile blankets or cushions around you.[46] When thunder roars, go indoors. Get into a building or a car with a roof.[48]

**What to avoid.** Stay away from windows, doors and outside walls.[46] There is no safe place in a car during a tornado, only less dangerous ones. If you are caught, stay buckled in and keep your head below the windows.[46] During a thunderstorm, avoid running water and electronics plugged into the wall.[48]

**How bad:** Severe (rough data).

### No grid power at home: about 5 days (up to 7 days)

**What helps.** A light for each person, a radio and phone power are in your plan; keeping food cold and charging up are on the forecast list; registries are under Local help.

**What to avoid.** Never run a generator inside your home or garage, even with the doors and windows open. Keep it outside, more than 20 feet from windows, doors and vents.[95] Put a carbon monoxide alarm on every level of your home.[96] Headache, dizziness, nausea or confusion can mean carbon monoxide poisoning. Get everyone outside to fresh air, then call 911.[97] Never heat your home with a gas stove or oven. Unplug electronics, because the power can come back with a surge that damages them.[96] Treat every downed power line as live: stay at least 30 feet from it and anything it touches, and call 911.[98] If one falls on your car, stay inside unless the car is on fire.[99]

The worst power cut in your region's records (where it was worst, about 75 miles (120 km) away) was Ice storm, February 2023; being ready for 5 days would have left some homes that lost power still waiting (about 20 in 100 of all customers there were still out).[6, 7, 10, 23, 50, 100, 101, 102]

### Tap water must be treated: about 10 days (3 days to 1 month)

**What helps.** Use bottled water, or bring clear water to a rolling boil for one minute. Boil for three minutes above 5,000 feet, then let it cool.[103] If you cannot boil water, add plain unscented bleach: 8 drops of 6% bleach or 6 drops of 8.25% bleach per gallon. Stir, and wait 30 minutes.[103] Use boiled or bottled water for drinking, cooking, brushing teeth, baby formula and ice. If the power is out too, a camp stove works, but only outdoors.[95]

**What to avoid.** Do not use water or ice from the fridge dispenser while a notice is on. Boil tap water even if it went through a home filter or a filter pitcher.[104] Boiling does not help if the notice warns of chemicals. That is a do-not-drink notice, and you need stored or bottled water instead.[104, 105]

This rounds up to 10 days: before rounding it is about 7.8 days, just past a week.[3, 6, 7, 9, 10, 23, 106, 107, 108, 109]

### No tap water at all: about 5 days (up to 2 weeks)

**What helps.** Store at least one gallon per person per day, for drinking and keeping clean.[1] Fill clean bottles or jugs with tap water and replace it every six months.[110] You can pick a level in the plan. About 3 liters a day covers drinking to survive, one gallon is the basic default, and about 4 gallons (15 liters) is the humanitarian minimum for drinking, cooking and washing.[111] A tank water heater holds 20 to 80 gallons of clean water.[112, 113] For long outages, a filter and a source of raw water go further than more jugs.[93] Filters do not remove viruses, so add a disinfectant such as chlorine dioxide after filtering.[105] A two-bucket toilet keeps waste safe when toilets cannot flush.[114]

**What to avoid.** Do not store water in containers that held chemicals.[110] Milk jugs seal poorly and turn brittle.[115] Never drink pool or spa water. Use it only for washing and cleaning.[113] After a flood, do not drink from a private well until it has been disinfected and tested. Your health department can tell you how.[116]

## Your shelter plan

Pick a spot for each danger below, at home and at work, and practice going there.[2]

**Strong wind.** In a high wind or severe thunderstorm warning, go inside a sturdy building, to an inside room or basement.[130] Stay away from windows while damaging wind is near.[131]

**Tornado.** A safe room or storm shelter is best; next is a small inside room with no windows on the lowest floor.[46] Even a tied-down mobile home is not safe.[47]

**Hurricane.** If officials tell your evacuation zone to leave, go right away. If you stay, use an inside room away from windows.[132]

**Chemical release.** If told to stay inside, go to an above-ground room with few openings. Close the windows, doors and vents, turn off fans and air conditioning, and seal the room with plastic sheeting and duct tape.[133]

**Smoke.** Make one room a clean room: close its windows and doors, and run an air cleaner that does not make ozone.[31]

**Radiation.** If officials warn of fallout, get inside, stay inside, stay tuned. Go to a basement or the middle of a brick or concrete building.[88]

## When a storm, freeze or heat wave is forecast

Hurricanes, winter storms and heat waves usually come with warning. Keep your phone charged when one is forecast, and use the time the same way each time.[132]

**Before any storm**

- Charge phones, power banks and other batteries.[134] 
- Fill the car's tank and get some cash, since card readers and cash machines need power.[134] If you would leave in an electric car, charge it fully.[135]
- Refill prescriptions if you can.[134]
- Fill the bathtub and other large containers with water for flushing and cleaning.[134]
- Turn the fridge to its coldest setting and keep the doors shut.[134] A full freezer keeps food cold for about 48 hours, a fridge for about four.[96]
- Bring in or tie down outdoor furniture and grills.[132]
- Check your evacuation zone and your plan to leave.[132]
- Check with neighbors, older adults and anyone who may need help.[132]

**Before a hard freeze.** Let hot and cold water drip from a faucet at night, open the cabinet doors under sinks on outside walls, and keep the heat at 55°F or higher. Make sure everyone knows how to shut off the water in case a pipe bursts.[39]

**Before a heat wave.** Pick a place to cool down, such as a library, or ask your local health department about cooling options. Plan to check on family, older adults and neighbors. Fans do not lower body temperature.[34]

## Access and functional needs

Planners group the needs a disaster makes harder under five headings, called CMIST: communication, maintaining health, independence, support and safety, and transportation.[145]

- **Prescription refills:** No state law allowing emergency refills was found in a 2022 review; in past disasters some governors allowed them by order. Ask your pharmacist.[151]

## Documents and money

Keep paper copies in a waterproof pouch and photos you can reach from any phone. FEMA's Emergency Financial First Aid Kit groups them in four parts.[45]

- [ ] **Who you are:** photo IDs, birth certificates, Social Security cards, passports, and pet records.
- [ ] **Money and legal papers:** insurance policies, the lease or deed, a will and powers of attorney, bank and card contact numbers (not PINs), and recent tax returns.
- [ ] **Medical papers:** insurance cards, the written medicine list, prescriptions, and vaccination records.
- [ ] **Contacts:** family, doctors, the insurance agent, the landlord or lender, and employers.

### Decisions

- [ ] **Decide: ID for every person (passport book or card, or a state ID).** A passport book or card for each person, children included, proves who you are and your citizenship if other papers are lost, and the card shows no home address; get them before you need them. The federal fee schedule: a first adult book $165 and card $65 ($130 and $30 plus a $35 acceptance fee), for children under 16 a book $135 and card $50 (22 CFR 22.1).[45, 152, 153]
- [ ] **Decide: homeowners, condo or renters insurance.** You have no renters insurance yet: get a quote and decide. Check what it pays if you have to live somewhere else for a while. (FEMA, Ready.gov)[45, 154]
- [ ] **Decide: flood insurance, even outside a flood zone.** Home and renters policies usually don't cover floods. Decide on flood insurance before you need it: Most homes in your county are outside the mapped high-risk flood zone, and that is where many uninsured floods happen: about 3 in 10 flood insurance claims come from outside high-risk flood areas. A quote costs nothing, and a new policy usually starts 30 days after you buy it. It pays up to $250,000 for the building and $100,000 for belongings, and renters can buy cover for belongings only. (FEMA, FloodSmart, Ready.gov)[9, 41, 154, 155, 156]
- [ ] **Decide: disability and life insurance for the people who earn.** Someone in your household earns money the others rely on: check whether your job offers disability insurance, and whether life insurance would carry the others through the years they would need. About 1 in 4 workers who start at 20 become disabled before retirement age. NAIC's buyer's guide helps you work out how much cover is enough. (SSA, NAIC)[62, 157]

### Cash

- Cash in small bills, kept with your documents, because ATMs and cards may not work in an outage: about $120: half of 3 days of your usual spending ($2,400 a month), the part that goes on food, fuel and medicine. No agency gives a dollar amount. (Ready.gov, FEMA; some amounts are estimates)[6, 7, 10, 23, 45, 49, 50, 136, 154]

### Savings

Of 100 households like yours, about 25 (10–40) will have an income gap of more than 3 months in the next 10 years. The goal is about 7 months of expenses (about $16,800); you have 0 months saved. Once your supplies plan is done, the same money can go here. This is a savings goal, kept separate from the supplies budget.

### If damage forces you out

If damage forced you out, 9 in 10 households like yours would be home again within about 3 months; living elsewhere that long costs about $2,300 at 30 % of your monthly spending, which loss-of-use insurance pays for.[6, 9, 10, 11, 36, 37, 38, 55, 158, 159]

## After a disaster: the first 30 days

**Your county.** Wayne County, Michigan had 2 federal major-disaster declarations in the last five full years.[160]

Recovery takes weeks. These steps come in rough order.

**Going home.** Go back only when local officials say it is safe. Do not go inside if you smell gas or the building looks damaged.[161] Run a generator only outside, more than 20 feet from windows, doors and vents.[95]

**Insurance and records.** Before you clean up, take photos and videos and make a list of the damage.[161] Keep every receipt.[162] Call your insurer as soon as you can, and an adjuster will come to inspect. Check the adjuster's estimate, and talk to them before you sign a repair contract.[163]

**Help from FEMA.** If a federal disaster declaration covers your county, apply at DisasterAssistance.gov or call 1-800-621-3362.[164] FEMA help does not replace insurance.[165]

**Scams.** FEMA never charges to apply or to inspect.[166] Its inspectors carry an official photo ID and never ask for your bank details; a FEMA shirt is not an ID.[162] Never sign your insurance check over to a contractor, and walk away from anyone who wants cash up front.[167]

**Medicine.** In a declared disaster, Medicare drug plans can help you find a pharmacy and replace lost medicine.[168] Many states let a pharmacist give an emergency supply when your prescriber cannot be reached, and the rules differ by state.[151] Healthcare Ready's Rx Open map shows which pharmacies are open in a disaster area.[169]

**Papers.** To replace lost IDs, start with your birth certificate, from the vital records office of the state where you were born.[170]

## Special needs

### Medicine

- 1 person takes prescription medicine every day: keep 21 days of it on hand. Keep a written list of each medicine, what it is for and the dose. After a disaster declaration some states let pharmacies give an emergency refill of up to 30 days, and many allow only a few days; ask your pharmacist what yours allows. (Florida DEM, CDC, Red Cross, Healthcare Ready)[3, 9, 10, 11, 53, 54, 60, 61, 151, 171, 172, 173, 174, 175]

### Antibiotics

- No antibiotics are included in this plan. If you have a specific, foreseeable need, such as remote travel, talk to your own clinician about a standby prescription with written instructions. Never use fish or pet antibiotics, never share prescriptions, and don't use expired ones. (CDC, FDA)[21, 22, 176, 177]

### Getting around

- 1 person may need help to leave quickly: arrange a ride and a helper now, and show them where the medicines and equipment are. (Ready.gov)[19, 148]

### Stress, mental health and the 988 line

**What helps.** Save 988 in every phone. It offers free, judgment-free support 24/7 for mental health, substance use and more, by call, text or chat.[178] After a disaster, the Disaster Distress Helpline offers crisis counseling 24/7 to anyone in emotional distress. Call or text 1-800-985-5990.[179] Write a short calm plan: what you might feel, what helps you, and who you will call.[180] Oregon's 2 Weeks Ready program even includes practicing mindfulness as a step in getting prepared.[181]

**What to avoid.** Do not keep the news on all day. No one, adult or child, benefits from graphic details or disturbing images.[182] Reach out before things feel unbearable. The 988 line supports people in emotional distress as well as in crisis.[178]
